question.text: What is STE-80, and how do its rules make a technical sentence easier to read?
question.known_at: Caption 1 says what it is. The how-question becomes clear only at caption 9 ('Some of the words do not help the reader').
question.result_stated: Yes, at caption 25: 'The goal is less work, not fewer words.' Caption 24 also says: 'The reader still fills the reservoir before starting the machine, with less work to read it.'

reply.motive: Reason to care: caption 6-7, 'Manuals are read under time pressure, often in a second language, so every word must help.' This reason covers manuals only. Nothing ties it to this reader's own technical text. Reason for the approach (keep the rules, drop the dictionary): missing.
reply.close: Partly. Caption 25, 'The goal is less work, not fewer words', states the general point. The video then ends on caption 26-27, 'STE-80 has more rules than these three…', a list of new rules, instead of returning to the opening question.
reply.recap: STE-80 is Simplified Technical English without the dictionary: use simple words, give instructions directly, and use action verbs. Those three rules turned a 16-word manual sentence into 'Fill the hydraulic reservoir before you start the machine.'
reply.strongest: Captions 18-22 (rule three): 'Make sure that it is full asks the reader to check a result. The verb fill names the action.' This gives a clear reason and a visible change.
reply.weakest: Captions 26-27: faint on-screen text and new rules that are never explained, at the point where the video should close. A runner-up is caption 10, 'Use simple words', which comes right after the video says the dictionary is dropped.
suggestions: Say how STE-80 judges a 'simple' word once the dictionary is gone, for example a common short word with one meaning.
Expand ASD (AeroSpace and Defence Industries Association of Europe), or leave it out.
Either drop the word-count bar or tell viewers early that it is only a rough stand-in for reading effort.
Say why 'the operator' becomes 'you': STE writes instructions in the imperative.
Move the noun change (operation → machine) out of the concrete-verb rule, or say that it is a separate fix.
End by restating the question and the answer, not with a list of new rules.
